publication: SAF-MCP: Secure Agentic Framework for Model Context Protocol (formerly SAFE-MCP), Framework Model v2

axioms.text: Adversary behavior against agentic systems follows the same 14 objectives as MITRE ATT&CK, from resource development and initial access through exfiltration and impact.
Attacker-controlled text, images, or audio that enter model context can make the model treat untrusted content as authoritative directions.
Adversaries hide instructions in an MCP tool description or parameter schema to steer the model's tool selection and arguments against the user's intent.
An MCP server can present a benign tool, gain approval, and later change that tool's metadata or code, so the host runs different behavior without new authorization.
Attacker-influenced output from one tool can drive a later call to a distinct tool or server that uses authority the agent already holds.
Content written into an agent's persistent memory can steer reasoning and tool decisions in a later session.
Repeated, equivalent approval requests can wear a user down until one is accepted, which defeats the human gate on a tool call or data disclosure.

invariables.text: The check that gates a privileged tool call must run in host code or with a human that the model cannot reach, prompt, or speak for.
Without a valid, unexpired, scope-matching authorization artifact, the host denies the privileged call; missing or malformed approvals never default to allow.
The authorization artifact must name the specific tool, its arguments or their digest, the requesting session, and a short expiry.
The right to request approval comes from the authenticated session role, never from text the model emitted or the user typed into the prompt.
Any tool interaction, resource access, or capability grant that is not explicitly permitted is blocked by default.
Privilege boundaries must be enforced at runtime during each tool execution as well as at configuration time, so revocations take effect immediately.
A detection rule that passes synthetic fixtures counts as fixture_tested and must not be represented as production effectiveness.

principles.text: Least privilege: the platform team grants each MCP tool the minimum privileges its function needs, so a compromised tool reaches only its granted scope.
Privilege isolation: the host keeps tools at different privilege levels apart and blocks a lower-privilege tool from invoking a higher one without escalation controls.
Control and data flow separation: the host takes control flow only from trusted queries and treats tool descriptions and API responses as data that cannot change execution.
Tool integrity: tool developers sign tool descriptions, and the client verifies the signature before it loads any tool.
Per-invocation capability brokering: a broker applies each tool's declared filesystem, network, and syscall manifest per call and issues a single-use token scoped to that call.
Complete audit trail: the host logs every privilege decision, escalation, grant, denial, and timeout with request context so reviewers can reconstruct who approved what.
principles.ref: SAF-M-29 Core Principles 4; SAF-M-69 Core Principles 5

principles.text: Defense in depth: operators layer architectural, prevention, detection, and response controls, starting with SAF-M-1, SAF-M-2, SAF-M-6, and SAF-M-11 when resources are limited.
principles.ref: MITIGATIONS.md, Defense in Depth Strategy and Priority Implementation

principles.text: Profile-scoped threat modeling: security teams select SAF Core plus the domain profiles that match their deployment, then map active techniques to their environment.
principles.ref: README.md, How to Use This Framework and Usage Guidelines

publication: Agent Privacy Risk Taxonomy V.01 (AILuminate Assessment Standard)

axioms.text: Traditional privacy models such as Solove's taxonomy and the NIST privacy risk model assume deterministic data flows, centralized storage, and clear perimeter boundaries.
Agents act as dynamic data intermediaries that execute code, keep memory across sessions, and orchestrate external tools and protocols such as MCP.
Agents favor task completion over data minimization, and MCP lacks field-level access controls that would limit the context shared with external tools.
Attackers embed hidden payloads such as invisible text, metadata, or system commands in emails, websites, and documents that agents process at run time.
Upstream agent components such as skill packages, tool descriptions, and MCP servers can be compromised to make an agent leak sensitive data during normal execution.
axioms.ref: p. 8, R2.4 Agentic supply chain manipulation

axioms.text: A constant stream of runtime permission pop-ups leads users to approve risky actions without reading, which removes the protection of the consent gate.
No standardized, scalable, privacy-preserving method exists for logging agent interactions across organizations, which slows root-cause analysis after an incident.

invariables.text: Intent-based inference of privacy preferences is probabilistic, so it cannot guarantee that an agent infers or follows a user's preferences in a provable way.
invariables.ref: p. 10, R4.1 Limitations in inferring and adhering to consent

invariables.text: Blocking an agent's access to one file or database does not stop it from reconstructing the restricted information through redundant or secondary sources.
invariables.ref: p. 7, R2.2 i. Beyond file-level privacy

invariables.text: A manipulated agent with a code execution tool such as a Python REPL or bash shell can bypass LLM-level privacy controls and gain read and write access to the host.
invariables.ref: p. 8, R2.5 Unauthorized access to data due to unexpected dynamic code execution

invariables.text: Regex and heuristic redaction pipelines fail to remove semantic PII and fuzzy quasi-identifiers, which can still re-identify users.
invariables.ref: p. 5, R1.5 Failure of traditional PII redaction techniques

invariables.text: Static, binary permission gates are structurally incompatible with the open-ended runtime reasoning of autonomous agents.
invariables.ref: p. 10, section 4 Failure of legacy consent systems

invariables.text: A successful attack, agent action, or technical data exposure does not by itself show that downstream harm occurred.

principles.text: Causal chain assessment: assessors trace each agent privacy risk from deployment condition or threat to failure mechanism, privacy event, affected party, privacy impact, and downstream harm.
Evidence labeling: the assessor states which stages of the causal chain were directly observed and which remain inferred or uncertain.
principles.ref: p. 13, "state which part of the causal chain was observed"

principles.text: Bounded likelihood: assessors give likelihood as a probability only when observed data has a defined population, denominator, and period; otherwise they rate exposure and failure separately.
Threat-conditioned failure evidence: assessors label each failure as seen in ordinary use, under a credible threat model with a defined attacker capability and budget, or plausible but unconfirmed.
Affected-party impact: assessors rate impact by its effect on affected parties, weighing data sensitivity, recipients, persistence, and reversibility, beyond technical compromise alone.

axioms.text: Offensive cyber operations often target unpatched or misconfigured systems, overly broad permissions, and weak credentials; attackers rarely need a sophisticated exploit.
Subverting an agent that guards a network could give an attacker broad, undetected access.
An agent's effectiveness depends heavily on the tools it can access, the software around the model that runs tools and manages memory, and its integration into the operating environment.
axioms.ref: p. 2, Agentic Capabilities and Security Tooling; footnote 1

axioms.text: As AI-reported vulnerabilities increase, triage becomes the bottleneck, and OT environments at critical infrastructure operators often cannot be patched on demand.
AI models can produce functionally correct code that still contains vulnerabilities such as unchecked memory allocation and missing input validation.
False positives consume analyst time, erode trust in automated systems, and cause alert fatigue that leads teams to overlook genuine threats.
Many existing cyber evaluations come from offensive security and measure success at discrete attack tasks, revealing little about defensive judgment.
axioms.ref: p. 7, Invest in Better Defensive Evaluations

invariables.text: Before agents receive greater autonomy, they must be hardened against prompt injection, data poisoning, and evasion attacks.
A defensive agent introduces risks of its own because the agent itself becomes a high-value target for attackers.
Finding a vulnerability is only a first step; organizations must be able to prioritize which ones to fix and develop deployable patches in a timely manner.
Applying a patch requires confirming existing functionality still works, testing compatibility with current systems, and coordinating downtime, which can take weeks or months.
Agentic code analysis and vulnerability discovery deliver far less value when strong authentication, timely patching, and vulnerability management are missing.

principles.text: Fundamentals first: organizations put strong authentication, timely patching, and disciplined vulnerability management in place before they invest in autonomous agents.
Staged deployment: security teams first automate alert triage, log analysis, and detection-rule drafting, then move to more transformative uses as confidence grows.
principles.ref: p. 6, Deploy in Stages and Match Autonomy to Risk

principles.text: Match autonomy to risk: the deploying organization sets each agent's autonomy by context and the consequence of error, granting more in lower-risk work such as code analysis.
principles.ref: p. 6, Deploy in Stages and Match Autonomy to Risk

principles.text: Zero trust: operators treat agents as untrusted components and constrain, log, and verify every agent action until agent security matures.
Synchronous monitoring: a separate LLM reviews each proposed agent action before it executes, alongside chain-of-thought monitoring of the agent's reasoning traces.
Human approval for consequential actions: escalation workflows route consequential agent decisions to a person, and agents work inside existing SOC tooling and playbooks.
Evidence-backed detections: red and blue team agents run commands against test systems that mirror production and validate each proposed detection rule against real log data.
Defensive evaluation under attack: evaluators test whether an agent makes sound decisions under uncertainty while adversaries are actively attacking.
principles.ref: p. 7, Invest in Better Defensive Evaluations

publication: AIMM: Artifact Integrity Maturity Model for AI/ML Supply Chain Trust and Provenance

axioms.text: An adversary can modify a model artifact between lifecycle stages, before it is uploaded to a hub, or before it is deployed.
Most AI models today move through their supply chains unsigned, unverified, and untraceable, and most externally sourced models are distributed without signatures.
axioms.ref: 11 Conclusion; 8 Incremental Adoption Strategies, 'Handling unsigned external models'

axioms.text: An attack or an honest mistake at any upstream transformation step can propagate undetected when consumers can verify only the final artifact in isolation.
Without signatures, provenance metadata is plain documentation that anyone can forge.
Model behavior cannot be determined through inspection, so consumers trust recorded evaluation results based on the identity of the attester who signed them.
The same organization often acts as a model consumer of foundation models and as a model producer of fine-tuned derivatives.
Many structured attestation schemas for domain compliance metrics do not exist yet or lack legal and standards review, so fully automated policy enforcement is still aspirational.

invariables.text: Any change to the bits of a signed model artifact invalidates its signature, provided the producer's signing system and keys show no sign of compromise.
Signing and attestation prove integrity and signer identity only; they do not prove that a model is correct, safe, fair, or benign.
A Level 1 signature is a point-in-time snapshot and cannot detect tampering that happens during a model transformation.
Each AIMM level inherits every lower-level control: Level 2 includes Level 1 integrity, and Level 3 includes integrity, lineage, and structured attestations.
The verification policy must map each role to the claim types it may produce, and verifiers reject any claim a party makes outside its authorized role.
Required attestations must be present and valid, and when independent parties compute different hashes for the same artifact, verification fails immediately.
When an orchestrator agent delegates artifact operations to a sub-agent, signing authority must not expand beyond the delegating principal's permissions.
Signing keys must be protected from unauthorized access, trust stores curated, and rotation and revocation procedures defined before they are needed.

principles.text: Sign at the release boundary: the model producer hashes the complete model artifact and signs the hash when training, fine-tuning, or packaging ends and the artifact is immutable.
Verify on download: the model consumer recomputes the hash and validates the signature, and rejects unsigned or invalidly signed models before they enter an ML pipeline or production.
Lineage by signature chaining: the producer signs each derived model with claims that cite the parent artifact's hash, and the verifier walks the chain and matches recorded hashes to real artifacts.
principles.ref: 5.2 Implementation Approach, 'Lineage tracking through signature chaining'

principles.text: Replay resistance: the verifier confirms each attestation signature is recent and non-replayable through trusted timestamping or short-lived certificates.
Admission gating: operators place a policy engine gate before deployment that blocks unsigned, unattested, or failing artifacts, with defined failover and break-glass steps for engine outages.

Risk-based adoption: the organization starts Level 1 on production, externally facing, or regulated models, adds Level 2 for derived models, and defers Level 3 until a policy and attestation tooling exist.
Re-sign at ingestion: when an external model arrives unsigned, the organization runs feasible integrity checks and signs it with its own key before admitting it to internal registries.
principles.ref: 8 Incremental Adoption Strategies, 'Handling unsigned external models'

principles.text: Defense in depth: the organization treats signing and attestation as one layer and pairs it with behavioral testing, runtime monitoring, and independent audits.

axioms.text: AI agents add and remove capabilities at runtime, such as a mid-session model swap, a hot-loaded MCP server, or a new A2A peer.
Enterprises cannot rely on black-box agents that operate across cloud, SaaS, on-premises, and endpoint environments.
An adversary who can disrupt the Guardian channel turns a fail-open control into audit only.
A Guardian that keeps its chain head private can drop an entry such as a DENY, recompute the chain forward, and later present a clean history.
When content is summarized, stored in memory, or passed across a boundary without its trust basis, asserted content can pass as attested; the spec calls this trust laundering.
A successful liveness ping does not show that enforcement works, since a Guardian can answer pings while rejecting every signed hook during a key outage.

invariables.text: The Observed Agent must wait for the Guardian's decision up to the negotiated timeout and apply it; a framework that emits hooks but ignores the verdict is not conformant.
Every agent step that proceeds without a Guardian decision must be recorded as an audit event, so the bypass is visible.
Provenance fields must be populated by deterministic framework code outside the LLM output path, and implementations must not instruct the LLM to produce them.
Every ACS-Core request and response carries a signature over the JCS-canonicalized envelope, with HMAC-SHA256 as baseline, and verifiers reject signatures that do not cover it.
invariables.ref: Instrument specification 10 Cryptographic Signatures; conformance.md ACS-Core

invariables.text: Guardians must reject requests that reuse a request_id within the session or carry a timestamp outside the negotiated skew window.
Once Intent.parsed is set, changes from the runtime LLM, tool outputs, or untrusted channels must be ignored or rejected; only an authenticated approver's ASK grant can extend it.
For every step that writes a ContextEntry, the Guardian must return the resulting chain_hash in its response, covered by the response signature.
A Guardian must not treat an asserted fact as attested, and agent-generated data labeled with trust takes the minimum trust of the data it derives from.

principles.text: Fail securely: a deployment that cannot accept fail-open sets on_decision_failure to deny, so an unreachable or silent Guardian blocks steps instead of letting them proceed.
principles.ref: Instrument specification 6.4; README, 'Two ways this breaks on the first try'

principles.text: Non-repudiation: a deployment that must prove which Guardian issued a decision or chain head adopts the ACS-Crypto profile, with ML-DSA-65 as the recommended algorithm.
Content-bound audit chain: the Guardian records request_hash, the SHA-256 of the canonical request params, on each ContextEntry so the chain commits to request content.
Inventory-aware policy: when policy depends on what an agent is built from, the agent sends an AgBOM snapshot before content hooks and an agbom/changed event on each hot-swap.
Recoverable escalation: for a client that cannot route ASK, the Guardian prefers DEFER with a deny timeout when the request may resolve elsewhere, and DENY when it is outside the client's authority.
Monitor the enforcement path: operators track hook-path decision failures directly instead of inferring Guardian health from system/ping responses.
Replayable policy state: the Guardian fills policy_references[].policy_version when audits or ledgers need to show which policy version produced a decision.
Verify vendor claims: a buyer tests a deployment against the ACS-Core requirements, because v0.1.0 conformance is self-declared and no test suite or registry checks it.

publication: GenAI Security Industry Framework Crosswalk v4.0.0

axioms.text: GenAI controls are spread across many frameworks, so a team deploying GenAI has to find and reconcile the controls that apply to each risk.
LLM application risks, agentic risks, and data security risks are distinct problem domains with different audiences, threat models, and mitigations.
One GenAI deployment can fall under several regimes at once, such as an EU payments chatbot under the EU AI Act, PCI DSS, ISO 27001, and DORA.
A mapping goes wrong quietly when a framework releases a new version and nobody rechecks the rows written against the old one.
Incident evidence counts reflect the incidents this project has recorded and reviewed, not the world, and lean toward failures that get publicly disclosed.
Removing human oversight raises average AIVSS severity by 1.79 points across the ten agentic entries and moves 7 of 10 from High to Critical.

invariables.text: Every mapping is unreviewed until a named human reviewer signs it, and an agent never adds itself to reviewed_by.
The validator fails any mapping whose confidence is above 'unreviewed' while its reviewed_by list is empty.
invariables.ref: docs/SCHEMA_V2_MIGRATION.md, 'A row may not claim review it does not have'

invariables.text: A control failure supports a mapping only when the incident lists that OWASP entry and names the same framework and control_id.
Only a confirmed control failure with a named confirmer counts toward evidence_count; drafted failures are shown but never counted.
A drafted failure needs a verbatim quote from a source stating that a control was missing or defeated; a description of the attack alone does not qualify.
A severity rating changes only with a cited AIVSS score, a CVSS score from a linked CVE, or the OWASP source list definition.
The incident index records only failures of deployed systems; lab attacks and proofs of concept against researcher-run systems are literature.
invariables.ref: docs/TRIAGE_RULES.md, 'The rule in one line' and Routing 1

invariables.text: Each mapping cites the authoritative framework text, not secondary summaries, and controls with only a tangential link to the risk are excluded.

principles.text: Tiered rollout: security teams apply Foundational controls first, in sprint 0 or 1, add Hardening controls in quarters 1 to 2, and reserve Advanced controls for high-risk or high-maturity settings.
Buy, build, or both: mapping authors tag each control by whether a vendor platform, internal engineering, or both deliver it, so teams can plan procurement and staffing.
Typed relationships: reviewers label each mapping with an OLIR relationship (equal, subset-of, superset-of, intersects-with, not-related-to) and a rationale naming the clause it reaches.
Version pinning: mapping authors record the framework release each row was written against, so drift between a mapping and a newer framework version is detectable.
Honest freshness: maintainers record mapped and upstream versions per framework and report unchecked frameworks apart from current ones, never merging the two states.
principles.ref: docs/FRESHNESS_SLA.md, Current state; How it is enforced

principles.text: Dispute resolution: when two mappings conflict, both proposers cite a primary source, the framework lead decides, and the losing evidence stays in a DISPUTE comment.
Deprecate, do not delete: maintainers mark a mapping DEPRECATED with a reason and remove it only with evidence that it is wrong.
principles.ref: GOVERNANCE.md, 'What the project will NOT do'

principles.text: Evidence-tiered scoring: the coverage scorer labels a result Self-Assessed, Partially Validated, or Tool-Validated based on uploaded Garak, PyRIT, LAAF, or compliance report evidence.

publication: Quantifying Agentic Misalignment in Multi-Agent Systems

axioms.text: LLM agents with enterprise tool permissions can pursue sub-goals that violate implicit safety policies even when every tool works as designed.
Once agents can send mail, modify files, and call APIs, the main risk moves from unsafe text to unsafe actions taken through trusted tools.
Agentic misalignment comes from the interaction of model, prompt, tool access, and adversarial context, so harm can occur without any conventional software exploit.
LLM-integrated systems struggle to separate trusted instructions from untrusted retrieved content, so an injected tool response can pass as task guidance.
Single-agent configurations acted on injected tool-response instructions in 93.3% to 100% of prompt_injection runs for all six tested models.
Misalignment varies sharply by model: overall rates across six models in the same 250-run matrix ranged from 7.6% to 41.2%.

invariables.text: Every tool output an agent receives must be handled as potentially hostile data and never as a trusted instruction.
invariables.ref: p. 8, Section 2.1 ("tool outputs must be treated as potentially hostile data"); p. 24, Recommendation 7

invariables.text: Prompt-level safety instructions alone do not secure a tool-using agent; runtime observability, tool-boundary controls, and scenario-specific validation are required alongside them.
Before production, deployers must log reasoning steps, tool strings, state transitions, and runtime actions so behavior is judged from artifacts rather than model self-report.
An agent's own transcript cannot prove what it did; misalignment is scored from durable artifacts left in the mail, file share, and API services it touched.
Automated scorer labels stay unvalidated until a manual audit checks scorer-positive and sampled scorer-negative runs against the raw service logs.
A 0% misalignment result in a cell with heavy timeout censoring is unresolved and cannot be reported as confirmed clean.
A low-risk result holds only for the tested model version, prompt, and tool configuration; it is not a durable safety guarantee after provider updates.

principles.text: Least privilege: the deploying team isolates email, SMB write, and administrative API access behind separate execution controls and tool-boundary checks for each agent.
Explicit tool constraints: the prompt author replaces broad task descriptions with enforceable rules, such as no emailing file contents and no admin endpoint calls outside the task.
Prompt-injection hardening: developers apply injection-resistant parsing to tool responses and treat returned content as data whenever an agent ingests external API output.
Behavior-first evaluation: security and AI governance teams test agents through sandboxed actions and the artifacts they leave before deployment, instead of reviewing static text output.
Isolated test environment: evaluation teams run agents in a non-production segment with synthetic data and test credentials, and route risky actions to capture sinks such as an SMTP trap.

Release gates: the agent owner sets thresholds such as maximum exfiltration attempt rate or STOP-ignore rate, requires evaluation at CI or release, and reruns it after major model, prompt, or tool changes.
Separate deception metric: evaluators score the gap between evaluation-framed and production-framed runs apart from base-rate misalignment before deployment.
Scenario-aware circuit breakers: operators set per-scenario timeout ceilings, longer for privilege escalation and multi-agent handoff tasks, because one global cutoff causes false interruption.

publication: MITRE ATLAS (Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems) v2026.09

axioms.text: Many moderation and filtering controls inspect mainly the text channel, so a payload hidden in an image, audio, video, or file metadata can still steer a multimodal model unnoticed.
axioms.ref: AML.T0129 Triggers in Multimodal Inputs (new in v2026.09)

axioms.text: Self-hosted AI runtimes listen on predictable ports and standard API paths, so attackers find model-serving hosts by scanning or by querying scan services such as Shodan and Censys.
axioms.ref: AML.T0006.002 Scan for Exposed AI Infrastructure; AML.T0000.003 Scan Databases (new in v2026.09)

axioms.text: Agent and SaaS platforms host agents behind URL patterns built from tenant, environment, or agent names, and default configurations keep those patterns the same across victims.
axioms.ref: AML.T0006.000 Enumerate Hosted AI Resources (new in v2026.09)

axioms.text: Most major AI assistants accept a prefilled prompt through a URL parameter such as ?q= or ?prompt=, so whoever controls a link can write the first turn of a user's conversation.
axioms.ref: AML.T0131 Crafted AI Assistant Links; AML.CS0072 description

axioms.text: Attackers who reach a working agent can map its tools, parameters, permissions, and embedded credentials at runtime by testing requests, without reading its configuration.
axioms.ref: AML.T0133 Discover AI Agent Runtime Capabilities (new in v2026.09)

axioms.text: Indirect prompt injection arrives through documents, email, databases, or websites the agent ingests, and the hijacked agent acts with whatever privileges the AI system holds.
Legitimate businesses also poison assistants: Microsoft found more than 50 memory manipulation prompts from 31 companies in about 60 days of email traffic, several aimed at health and finance.
axioms.ref: AML.CS0072 AI Recommendation Poisoning via Crafted AI Assistant Links (new case study)

invariables.text: Any agent whose context takes in untrusted data can have its tools invoked by prompt injections in that data, with confidentiality, integrity, or availability violations as the result.
invariables.ref: AML.M0030 Restrict AI Agent Tool Invocation on Untrusted Data

invariables.text: Production models require users to verify identity, API endpoints require authentication, and operators monitor model queries against usage policy.
invariables.ref: AML.M0019 Control Access to AI Models and Data in Production

invariables.text: Validation of inputs and outputs for agent tools and data sources runs outside the AI agent, covering schema checks, leakage checks, and removal of injections or unsafe code.
invariables.ref: AML.M0033 "Validation should be performed external to the AI agent"

invariables.text: A human decision maker gives final approval of agent actions; audit agents may assist the review but do not replace the human approver.
invariables.ref: AML.M0029 Human In-the-Loop for AI Agent Actions

invariables.text: Agent execution environments start from a clean base image on each run and carry forward no operational state.
invariables.ref: AML.M0032 Segmentation of AI Agent Components

invariables.text: Defenders verify the cryptographic checksum of every AI artifact to confirm an attacker did not modify the file.
Any interaction with a decoy AI service, agent, or credential signals unauthorized activity with high confidence, because authorized users and workflows have no reason to touch it.

principles.text: Deception with AI honeypots: the security team places monitored decoy AI services, agents, and credentials beside real assets and feeds captured prompts and tooling into detection rules.
principles.ref: AML.M0039 AI Honeypots; mitigates AML.T0006.000 to .003, AML.T0132, AML.T0133

principles.text: Least privilege: the deploying team grants a privileged or multi-user agent only the tools and resources its designated task requires, enforced with RBAC or ABAC.
principles.ref: AML.M0026 Privileged AI Agent Permissions Configuration

principles.text: Delegated access: the platform team gives each tool shared across agents the permissions, identity, and limits of the calling agent, set in the MCP server or tool configuration.
principles.ref: AML.M0028 AI Agent Tools Permissions Configuration

principles.text: Consequence-scaled confirmation: once untrusted data enters an LLM's context, the system blocks automatic tool calls or asks the user to confirm, and always asks for high-consequence actions.
principles.ref: AML.M0030 Restrict AI Agent Tool Invocation on Untrusted Data

principles.text: Staged guardrails: developers check prompts, retrieved context, tool calls, and outputs at each workflow stage, log each guardrail decision, and add observed failures to evaluation datasets.
principles.ref: AML.M0020 Generative AI Guardrails (updated in v2026.09)

principles.text: Agent telemetry: operators log model inputs and outputs and, for agents, intermediate steps, data access, tool use, install commands, and the agent's identity.
Threat-informed red teaming: an AI red team runs recurring authorized exercises against models, data, agent memory and tools, and data flows before deployment and during operation.

publication: ETSI TS 104 275 V1.1.1: Securing Artificial Intelligence (SAI); Application of Baseline Cyber Security Requirements for AI Models and Systems principles to Generative AI; Preventing Harm from Deepfakes

axioms.text: AI differs from traditional software through risks such as data poisoning, model obfuscation, and indirect prompt injection, plus differences in how data is managed.
Deepfakes have been used to sway elections and to create non-consensual pornography, child sexual abuse material, low-cost deepfake adverts, and synthetic terrorist content.
Deepfake harm falls into three groups: psychological (extortion, defamation), financial (identity theft, fraud, stock manipulation), and societal (election manipulation, national security).
The harms, threats, and mitigations that apply to GenAI also apply to Agentic AI, which the specification treats as an evolution of GenAI.
Simple changes to how a deepfake is produced can sharply cut detector reliability, and compression on social platforms removes the pixels and artefacts detectors depend on.
Manual deepfake detection by a skilled reviewer works for small volumes but cannot keep up with the volume of audio-visual material shared today.
Victims of non-consensual deepfakes see the same content reappear on many sites and have to request formal removal each time.

invariables.text: System Operators and Developers shall give users training on GenAI deepfake threats; the conformance test fails if that training content was not reviewed in the last 12 months.
The GenAI user interface shall encourage responsible use through content filters, clear labels on AI-generated content, and notices about limits on output reliability and accuracy.
Operators and Developers shall complete a risk assessment and implement and verify required mitigations before a GenAI system is deployed, with residual risks documented and approved.
Operators and Developers shall keep human oversight of a deployed GenAI system, monitor it, and implement tracked updates when risks materialize.
Developers, Operators, and Data Custodians shall get informed consent before training or adapting GenAI on a user's works, and the system shall enforce opt in or opt out at any time.
The Developer shall confirm that GenAI training data was legally accessed or licensed; incomplete data lineage or missing license evidence fails conformance.
An organization shall have a risk communication policy that covers its roles, statutory duties, escalation paths, and information sharing with authorities such as a Market Surveillance Authority.

principles.text: Continuous risk research: System Operators and Developers review safety and security research on a set cadence, for example quarterly and not only after incidents, and track decisions, owners, and actions.
principles.ref: p. 11, Provision 5.1.3.-1; p. 22, C.2.3.1 Pass verdict

principles.text: Multilingual red teaming: Developers and System Operators send the same harmful prompt in several languages and add controls when any version produces harmful output.
Cross-verification: System Operators and Developers check GenAI outputs against trusted external sources, and the human oversight process responds to incorrect outputs and hallucinations.
Infringement testing: the Developer generates sample images or text, runs reverse image or text searches for infringing matches, and adds measures to stop repeats.
Security transparency: Developers and System Operators tell GenAI users what steps they take to secure infrastructure and the supply chain.
principles.ref: p. 12, clause 5.2.2 NOTE and clause 5.2.3 NOTE

principles.text: Patch notification: Developers and System Operators keep a policy that informs users about security updates, patches, and threat mitigations as they are applied.
Privacy-preserving training: developers apply federated learning, differential privacy, and model anonymization where anonymization does not compromise the model's intended purpose.
principles.ref: p. 19, Table B.1 Requirement 3 Privacy and data governance

principles.text: Data subject rights at end of life: Developers and System Operators set up processes that honor end-user GDPR rights of access (Art. 15), erasure (Art. 17), and portability.
